title: Asymmetric Light Scattering from an Atomic System with Gain: A Quantum Analysis
abstract: We study the the scattering of light by a binary system of identical atoms in which one of them is incoherently pumped. This system belongs to the kind of non-parity symmetric optical systems in which gains and losses are partially compensated. We carry out a fully quantum analysis of the directionality of the radiation scattered from the atoms when the incident light strikes the system either perpendicular or alongside the interatomic axis. We find that, generally, while the degree of asymmetry depends on the pump rate, the preferred direction for emission depends on the interatomic distance and the detuning of the probe field with respect to the resonant frequency. On physical grounds, for the case of frontal illumination, the asymmetry is the result of the interference of the photons emitted from different atoms. On the contrary, for side lighting, the asymmetry with respect to the side of incidence is caused by both the phase difference between the probe field photons that strike each atom and the interference between the photons emitted from different atoms. Further, for side lighting too, our quantum approach demonstrates that the forward scattered power depends on the side of incidence, which reveals the lack of reciprocity in the quantum optical response of the system. This result conflicts with what is obtained within a classical approach.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes asymmetric light scattering from a two-atom system incorporating optical gain. Using advanced quantum diagrammatic techniques, the authors demonstrate that the resulting optical response is fundamentally non-reciprocal—a feature absent in classical models. This highlights how quantum interference effects dictate directional properties when gain and loss are present.
main_problem: The study investigates the directionality and asymmetry of light scattering from a two-atom system containing gain, focusing on how this response deviates from classical predictions.
main_result: The fully quantum analysis reveals non-reciprocity in the optical response (forward power depending on the side of incidence), which contradicts classical linear response theory. This asymmetry is linked to interference effects involving phase differences and inter-atom emission.
method: The authors employ a full quantum mechanical, diagrammatic perturbation theory approach using time-ordered Green's functions to calculate vacuum expectation values of quadratic field fluctuations.
model_or_system: The system consists of two identical three-level atoms forming a dimer, where one atom is incoherently pumped (gain). The interaction is analyzed under weak probe fields ($\Omega_0$) and involves considering both single-atom and collective scattering processes.
key_observables: Differential scattered power $W(	heta)$, the ratio of forward/backward scattered powers ($W^G/W^L$), and the dependence on illumination geometry (frontal vs. side lighting).
important_parameters: Pump rate ($P$), interatomic distance ($k_R$), probe detuning ($\Delta = \omega - \omega_0$), and the relative phase factors associated with side incidence.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on perturbative expansions in the interaction Hamiltonian, integrating out fast dynamics of auxiliary states, and assuming specific limits for time evolution (e.g., $\gamma t \gg 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate angular distributions ($W(	heta)$) for both frontal and side illumination geometries, comparing quantum predictions against classical models using log-ratio plots.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the physical model and Hamiltonian to calculating scattering power via diagrammatic expansion. It systematically compares results for different illumination geometries (frontal vs. side) and contrasts the fully quantum findings with those derived from classical linear response theory, highlighting points of divergence.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes beyond standard semiclassical treatments in quantum optics by rigorously demonstrating fundamental non-reciprocal effects arising purely from quantum interference and gain/loss mechanisms in open systems.
